newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end down as worry grows, jobs loom.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end down as worry grows, jobs loom.

text.p: U.S. Treasury securities prices ended lower Wednesday after as-expected results from a central bank meeting were followed by a rise in bearish sentiment.

The Federal Reserve's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) said it left monetary policy unchanged -- exactly where it's been for a year now -- at the conclusion of its two-day meeting in Washington.
The 30-year long bond ended 20/32 lowerr at 96-23/32. Its yield rose to 6.76 percent from 6.71 percent late Tuesday and attention immediately shifted to January's payrolls report.

Treasuries took a battering after the results of the FOMC's deliberations were made known, as rumors of central bank intervention weighed on the market and some volatility was reflected in the Treasury hiking the size of its inflation-indexed 10-year bond at the quarterly refunding auction next week.

John Canavan, analyst at Stone & McCarthy Research Associates wasn't sure the change by Treasury had that large an effect, but said there was some pickup in activity after the FOMC meeting ended. Overall activity was choppy throughout the afternoon but still below average levels, he said.

Traders said many investors were becoming increasingly antsy ahead of the payrolls report on Friday, fearing the market had been oversold recently. Yields on the 30-year long bond had fallen to 6.71 percent at Tuesday's close from 6.94 percent as recently as January 27.

"The focus now is on the employment report and the concern is it could be strong and that would take some of the exuberance out of the market," said John Williams, chief global markets economist at Bankers Trust Co.
A Reuters consensus called for the creation of 237,000 payrolls and a 5.2-percent jobless rate.

"If the (number prints an increase of) 250,000 I guess the markets probably will be okay, but I don't think they should be," Williams said. "I think this economy's on the verge of overheating and a 250,000 increase would be consistent with that."
Williams said he thought the market was remarkably complacent in the face of building inflationary pressures that should surface by the spring and force a tightening.
"People may be overstating the degree to which this number may be explained away by seasonal adjustments," Williams warned. "If the number looks strong, it is strong."

Carol Stone, senior economist at Nomura Securities International Inc., said the increase in the size of the 10-year added supply concerns to the marketplace. But she also noted that trading volume wasn't very heavy and cautioned against drawing too much from the late afternoon dropoff.

"Volume wasn't very large and there were just no buyers out there to offset the price declines we saw," Stone said. "The truth is we're all sitting around biting our nails worried about the employment number on Friday."
The Dow Jones Industrial Average also fell sharply with the DJIA ending 86 points lower.

As expected, the Fed did not intervene in the banking system Wednesday during its usual midmorning period. Fed funds closed the session at 5.25 percent, right at the Fed's current official target level.

Also on Wednesday, the two-year note was down 1/32 at 99-31/31 and yielded 5.89 percent; the five-year closed down 5/32 at 100-4/32 and yielded 6.22 percent, and the 10-year note closed down 9/32 at 100-7/32 to yield 6.47 percent.
